---
title: "Quiz: point patterns and complete spatial randomness"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Intensity ρ = points per µm².

---

**Q1.** A point pattern is "positions + window + marks". Why is the window part of the data? Give an example where getting it wrong changes the conclusion.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where could a point have been, but was not?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
"No point here" is only information where we looked. Cells in a tissue section that fills half of the image look strongly clustered if the whole image is taken as the window: half of it is empty glass. The intensity n/|W| is also halved. Use the tissue mask as the window.
:::

---

**Q2.** You detect spots in a widefield image where the PSF is wide. Will the detected pattern look more clustered or more regular than the true molecules? And if nuclei are over-segmented?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to two spots closer than the PSF width?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Close spots merge into one detection, so short distances disappear: the pattern looks **more regular**. Over-segmented nuclei give two points a few µm apart: extra short distances, the pattern looks **more clustered**.
:::

---

**Q3.** State the two properties of complete spatial randomness. Which one makes it easy to simulate?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Counts in a region; counts in two regions.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(1) The count in any region A is Poisson with mean ρ|A|. (2) Counts in non-overlapping regions are independent. Together they imply that, given n points in W, the points are n independent uniform positions: simulate by drawing n uniform points (rejection sampling in a mask).
:::

---

**Q4.** Cells are counted in 25 quadrats: mean 4, variance 12. What is the VMR, and what does it suggest? What would a VMR of 0.3 suggest?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Under CSR the counts are Poisson.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
VMR = 12/4 = 3: much more variable than Poisson, so clustered at the scale of the quadrats (some quadrats full, many nearly empty). VMR 0.3: counts are more even than chance: regular.
:::

---

**Q5.** Colonies of cells, each cell keeping a distance from its neighbours: with 5 µm quadrats the VMR is 0.9, with 20 µm quadrats 3.0. Which is right?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two mechanisms, two scales.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both. At the scale of a cell the pattern is regular (cells have a size and do not overlap); at the scale of a colony it is clustered. A single number describes one scale only, which is why the next units use functions of the distance.
:::

---

**Q6.** Cells are denser near a blood vessel but do not interact with each other. Is this pattern CSR? Is it "clustered"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
First order or second order?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is not CSR, because the intensity is not constant. It is an inhomogeneous Poisson pattern: quadrats and the plain K function will report "clustered", but there is no interaction between cells. Unit 5 separates the two.
:::

---

**Q7.** What does the bandwidth σ of a kernel intensity estimate do? Why divide by the blurred window?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Recall Gaussian smoothing.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
σ is the scale of "density": small σ gives a bump at each point, large σ gives nearly a constant. Near the border part of each Gaussian falls outside the window, so the sum is too low; dividing by the blurred window indicator e(**x**) puts the missing mass back.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that for a Poisson process with intensity ρ, the probability that a disc of radius r is empty is $e^{-\rho\pi r^2}$. With ρ = 0.004 µm⁻², what is it for r = 10 µm?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Poisson probability of 0 events.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$N(\text{disc}) \sim \text{Poisson}(\rho\pi r^2)$ and $P(N = 0) = e^{-\rho\pi r^2}$. With ρπr² = 0.004 · 314.2 = 1.26: $e^{-1.26} = 0.28$.
:::
